content:
Managing an observability stack often feels like a constant battle between performance and cost.
The example case is we are looking for reliable, powerfull, and fast log query performance. The top of mind stack is Elasticsearch (ELK Stack). But as log volumes grow, the reality of managing it sets in: the compute costs for RAM and CPU become massive, and SSDs become a requirement just to keep the indexing from lagging under pressure.
Alternative way to cut the cost, many shift toward Grafana Loki. It feels like a major win at first because logs can be offloaded to shared external object storage like S3 or MinIO, significantly cutting storage overhead. Plus, it integrates perfectly with the Grafana ecosystem — Prometheus, Alloy, and OpenTelemetry.
However, a new wall eventually appears: query performance. When dealing with unstructured data or high-cardinality logs with many unique labels. Complex filtering that should take seconds often takes minutes, which is exactly what is not needed during a critical incident.
I was intrigued by ClickHouse’s claim of being a columnar database. In theory, this allows for lightning-fast filtering on high-cardinality logs while still keeping the storage benefits of Loki, as ClickHouse natively supports S3 backends. To make it even better, I found ClickStack, which bundles HyperDX — a UI that gives you that familiar Kibana.
Note: This is a setup guide based on my curiosity. I’m not presenting a final benchmark yet, but rather a walkthrough of how I got this stack running to see if it lives up to the hype.
Moving forward, let’s dive into the topology and thes setup steps. This design is built to ensure each component scales independently.
Prerequisite and Setup
MinIO as external storage for ClickHouse. You can use other S3 object storage, like AWS S3 or GCS. In this post I won’t explain how to setup the MinIO, you can follow this guide to setup using Helm. Altinity ClickHouse operator, to deploy ClickHouse with High Availability setup. OpenTelemetry collector, to collect Kubernetes logs and forward to clickhouse. ClickStack, to deploy HyperDX UI with Helm chart. Step 1: Deploy ClickHouse Operator The first step is to install the Altinity ClickHouse Operator. This operator simplifies defining complex ClickHouse clusters — including shards, replicas, and keepers.
Optionally, prepare the Helm values for Altinity ClickHouse Operator. In this case, I will add specific namespace to watch the CRD, because I will deploy it on logging namespace.
configs: files: config.yaml: watch: namespaces: - logging helm repo add altinity https://helm.altinity.com helm install clickhouse-operator altinity/altinity-clickhouse-operator -n clickhouse --create-namespace -f altinity-values.yaml Verify that the operator is running:
ubuntu@ubuntu-1:~$ kubectl get po -n clickhouse NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE clickhouse-operator-altinity-clickhouse-operator-f86457cb6bz7xj 2/2 Running 0 3m27s Step 2: Provisioning ClickHouse Cluster with S3 Backend Before continuing to deploy the ClickHouse, you need to prepare the bucket and access credential to the bucket, which access_key_id &amp; secret_access_key.
Once the operator is ready and the bucket has been created, we can deploy the ClickHouse cluster. In this setup, I am using a High Availability configuration (2 shards, 2 replicas) integrated with MinIO object storage.
--- apiVersion: &#34;clickhouse-keeper.altinity.com/v1&#34; kind: &#34;ClickHouseKeeperInstallation&#34; metadata: name: ch-logging-keeper namespace: logging spec: configuration: clusters: - name: &#34;ch-cluster&#34; layout: replicasCount: 3 --- apiVersion: &#34;clickhouse.altinity.com/v1&#34; kind: &#34;ClickHouseInstallation&#34; metadata: name: ch-logging namespace: logging spec: configuration: zookeeper: nodes: - host: &#34;keeper-ch-logging-keeper.logging.svc.cluster.local&#34; port: 2181 clusters: - name: &#34;ch-cluster&#34; layout: shardsCount: 2 replicasCount: 2 settings: …
summary: Managing an observability stack often feels like a constant battle between performance and cost.
title: Kubernetes Logs Observability with ClickStack — ClickHouse & HyperDX

content:
There are lots of open source CI/CD tools out there. Most of CI tools that I know is possibly triggering build by manual trigger, event trigger, or scheduled trigger. But I haven’t found a CI tool that can ensure that code that is pushed will always be tested, if it doesn’t pass it never will.
And I found this concept https://gating.dev/
Every change is built and tested or it doesn’t merge
Project gating have some advantage rather than manually trigger build. And the implementation is suitable to ensure that every change is thoroughly tested before it is merged into our main repository code. Based on that curiosity, then found this CI tool that has standout features for its project gating capability.
But it also has its drawbacks, like its a bit tricky if you want to rebuild the existing one.
Zuul CI is part of OpenInfra project https://openinfra.dev/projects/. One of the opensource foundation that focusing on development of open infrastructure.
Key Features One of the standout features of Zuul CI is its project gating capability. This ensures that only changes that pass all tests are merged. To put it simply — stop merging broken code!
Zuul CI runs the CI/CD using Ansible. With Ansible makes Zuul CI highly customizable and flexible in defining and running jobs. And you can use the same Ansible playbooks to deploy your system and run your tests.
It is also have shared defined Ansible for Zuul on this, then you not require to start it from zero https://opendev.org/zuul/zuul-jobs/src/branch/master.
Then it support cross-repository dependencies, which allows us testing changes across multiple repositories. Multi-system gating (infrastructure
to apps, multi-project, multi-cloud).
https://zuul-ci.org/
Integrating Zuul with Kubernetes Nodepool is a system for managing test node resources. It supports launching single-use test nodes from cloud providers as well as managing access to pre-defined pre-existing nodes. In this case I want to use Kubernetes as the nodepool providers.
providers: - name: k3s driver: kubernetes context: default pools: - name: main labels: - name: pod-python type: pod image: docker.io/python - name: pod-k8s-util type: pod image: docker.io/bagas25/k8s-util:latest - name: pod-dind type: pod spec: containers: - name: pod-dind securityContext: privileged: true image: docker.io/bagas25/dind:latest So to use kubernetes as the nodepool, you need to configure it through providers configuration section.
Simply you can create labels for your pool and put your Pod specification inside the labels. Then your builds can run on those node.
The important things to integrate with Zuul is you need to provide cluster access to Zuul. It is require to add cluster config on Zuul machine.
Or optionally you can deploy the Zuul inside your K8s cluster. Some option available is using Zuul helm-chart or Zuul Kubernetes Operator.
Connecting to Repository Zuul support integration to common repositories, like GitHub, GitLab, Gerrit. For GitHub, you need to add the connection first by creating GitHub app integration and configure it on Zuul configuration
zuul.conf [connection &#34;zuullab&#34;] driver=github webhook_token=&lt;token&gt; app_id=&lt;app_id&gt; app_key=/etc/zuul/github.pem After successfully integrate to GitHub, make sure it can connect to GitHub. You can check it out on your App Integration settings.
Then, last you need to add the source on your Zuul tenant configuration. This sections, you can select which repository that will set as the project on Zuul.
main.yaml - tenant: name: zuul-lab source: zuullab: config-projects: - bagaswibowo25/zuul-config: load-branch: main untrusted-projects: - bagaswibowo25/sample-flask-app - bagaswibowo25/flask-charts Setup the Projects After connecting to the repository, you need to define the workflow of your projects.
- project: name: ^.*$ check: jobs: [] gate: jobs: [] - project: name: zuul-config check: jobs: - noop gate: jobs: - noop On this project settings, allows you to define the …
summary: There are lots of open source CI/CD tools out there.
title: Effortless Kubernetes Delivery with Zuul CI

content:
Helm is very useful to package your application. It have capability to templating your Kubernetes resources. So you can reuse the same resource for different purpose. Besides it will help you or developer to maintain the resource with simpler structure kind of resource based on Helm best practices or with your own way.
In this part I will try to templating the Network Policy resources by Helm. The first problem is Network Policy can be a complex resource to manage and hard to understand.
To ensure security for your application the Network Policy was very important, you will control the incoming and outgoing traffic from nor to your application. First you need to understand the flow of Network Policy to identify what need to do to ensure your application is secure.
Network Policy Editor by Cilium
The tool that very helpful for me is https://editor.networkpolicy.io/. It will help you to generate the Network Policy with your own needs. So why we still need the Helm to templating the Network Policy?
After we applying the Network Policy we still need to maintain the rule that we apply to the cluster. If we apply the complex rule and manage multiple application will hard to maintain. So we can simplify it by using Helm.
Below the manifest of Network Policy that templated using Helm.
networkpolicy.yaml
{{- range .Values.networkPolicies }} apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: {{ .name }} spec: {{- include &#34;netpol.podSelector&#34; . | indent 2 }} {{- if .ingress }} {{- include &#34;netpol.ingress&#34; . | indent 2 }} {{- end }} {{- if .egress }} {{- include &#34;netpol.egress&#34; . | indent 2 }} {{- end }} --- {{- end }} Looks simpler than original resource right? By that template Helm can generate multiple Network Policy file by just passing the value that we required to apply the policy. The main key of the Network Policy is Ingress and Egress and the components to control the traffic is:
Outside cluster, later we can define it by name cidrs. This part will control the traffic coming from nor to outside cluster by IP block subnets. In Namespace, later we can define it by name podSelectors. This part will control the traffic inside the namespace where the application is deployed. It will control the access between the application within the namespace. In Cluster, later we can define it by name namespaceSelectors. This part will control the traffic within the cluster, thats why I defined as namespaceSelectors. Because the traffic will be scoped within cluster and can be filtered per-namespace. With namespaceSelectors also we still need to define the specific Pod labels to apply the rule. All the components of Network Policy will be created through the named template, is simply a template defined inside the file. By default defined inside _helpers.tpl on the templates directory. You can read more detail to understand the Helm flow control here https://helm.sh/docs/chart_template_guide/control_structures/
Let’s look into the inside _helpers.tpl:
Create a function to handle the podSelector {{- define &#34;netpol.podSelector&#34; }} {{- if .podSelector }} podSelector: {{- range $key, $value := .podSelector }} matchLabels: {{ $key }}: {{ $value }} {{- end }} {{- else }} podSelector: {} {{- end }} {{- end }} On those part, the template will handle to define which resource that will be applied by the policy. If not defined will set the podSelector: {}, it mean the policy applied to all Pod inside the namespace.
2. Create a function to generate the Ingress and Egress section
{{/* Ingress block */}} {{- define &#34;netpol.ingress&#34; }} ingress: - from: {{- if .ingress.cidrs }} {{- with .ingress }} {{- include &#34;netpol.scoped.cidr&#34; (dict &#34;scope&#34; .) | indent 2 }} {{- end }} {{- end }} {{- if .ingress.podSelectors }} {{- with .ingress }} {{- include &#34;netpol.scoped.podSelector&#34; (dict &#34;scope&#34; .) | indent 2 }} {{- end }} {{- end }} {{- if .ingress.namespaceSelectors }} {{- with …
summary: Helm is very useful to package your application.
title: Helm — Templating Network Policy using Helm
